claims.text: A dense, continuous spinel-type oxide film formed during high-temperature processing governs resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion in high-entropy alloys.
The protective oxide film is rich in elements such as Al and Fe.
The oxide film prevents penetration of corrosive ions and reduces mechanical material removal.
The starting alloy is nanocrystalline and has a homogeneous elemental distribution without significant surface enrichment or preformed oxide layers.
Sintering at approximately 1000 °C promotes selective surface enrichment.
Sintering at approximately 1000 °C triggers formation of a compact, continuous spinel-type surface oxide.
The relevant comparison uses alloys sintered at 1000 °C and at 850–950 °C and evaluates corrosion in 3.5 wt% NaCl.
Alloys processed at 850–950 °C do not form the same complete, adherent protective oxide film as alloys processed at 1000 °C.
High-temperature sintering causes selective segregation of Al and Fe at the surface, followed by in situ oxidation into a spinel-type film.
The oxide film increases surface hardness.
The oxide film provides high electrical or electrochemical resistance and acts as a barrier to corrosive species.
The oxide film resists spallation during simultaneous wear and corrosion.
Alloys processed at 1000 °C have lower corrosion current density and higher film resistance than alloys processed at 850–950 °C.
Alloys processed at 1000 °C have significantly lower wear rates than the lower-temperature baseline.
Total degradation under simultaneous wear and corrosion is lower for the 1000 °C processed alloy than for the lower-temperature baseline.
Lower-temperature baseline alloys undergo a direct-attack corrosion mechanism and greater wear because they have less surface reinforcement.
The protective effect should persist under moderate loads while the oxide film remains intact.
The protective effect can fail at loads sufficient to spall the film or in environments aggressive enough to overcome its barrier effect.
